units.title: The West and the Gilded Age (1865 to 1898)
units.blurb: The railroads and the West, wars on the Plains and the policy of assimilation, big business, workers and unions, new immigrants and cities, politics and the Populists, Jim Crow and the debates of the age. AP Period 6.

units.title: Empire and the Progressive Era (1890 to 1920)
units.blurb: The U.S. as a world power, the Progressive reformers and presidents, new amendments, women's suffrage, the Great Migration and the First World War. AP Period 7.

units.title: The 1920s and the Great Depression (1920 to 1941)
units.blurb: A new mass culture and its conflicts, the Crash, life in the Depression, the New Deal and its critics, and the road to war. AP Period 7.

units.title: World War II (1941 to 1945)
units.blurb: Pearl Harbor, the home front, the incarceration of Japanese Americans, the war in Europe and the Holocaust, the war in the Pacific and the atomic bombs, and planning the peace. AP Period 7.

units.title: The Cold War (1945 to 1991)
units.blurb: Containment, the Red Scare, Korea, the 1950s, Kennedy and Cuba, Vietnam, the Great Society, Nixon and Watergate, and the end of the Cold War. AP Periods 8 and 9.

units.title: The Civil Rights Movement (1940s to 1970s)
units.blurb: Early victories, Brown v. Board, Montgomery, sit-ins and freedom rides, the great civil rights laws, the debates within the movement, and other movements for equal rights. AP Period 8.

units.title: The Last Decades of the Century (1970s to 2000)
units.blurb: The 1970s, the conservative resurgence, a world after the Cold War, the technology revolution and the politics of the 1990s, told as dated facts with each side's view. AP Period 9.

topics.title: The Transcontinental Railroad
topics.short: The first transcontinental railroad was finished at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869, built largely by Chinese workers from the west and Irish and other workers from the east, and backed by federal land grants and loans.
topics.trouble: Students think private companies built the railroads on their own. Congress gave the Union Pacific and Central Pacific millions of acres of land and government bonds.

topics.title: Wars on the Plains
topics.short: As settlers, miners and railroads moved west and the bison herds were destroyed, the U.S. Army fought Plains nations: Sand Creek (1864), the Little Bighorn (1876), and the killing of Lakota people at Wounded Knee (1890); most nations were confined to reservations.
topics.trouble: Students think Plains nations simply lost every battle or were never at war with each other's rivals. Native victories such as the Little Bighorn happened; what decided the outcome was the loss of the bison, disease, and the numbers and supplies of the Army.

topics.title: Assimilation and the Dawes Act
topics.short: Policy shifted to assimilation: boarding schools such as Carlisle (1879) separated children from their languages and cultures, and the Dawes Act (1887) split reservation land into family plots, with the "surplus" sold; Native landholding fell from about 138 to 48 million acres by 1934.
topics.trouble: Students think the Dawes Act gave Native people more land. It broke up land held in common, and most of the land left Native hands; it ended with the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

topics.title: Big Business and Industry
topics.short: Steel (Andrew Carnegie, the Bessemer process), oil (John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil), electricity and the telephone transformed the economy; firms grew by vertical and horizontal integration and trusts, and the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed combinations in restraint of trade.
topics.trouble: Students mix up vertical and horizontal integration. Vertical means owning each stage of making one product (mines, mills, railroads); horizontal means buying up competitors at the same stage.

topics.title: Workers and Unions
topics.short: Workers faced long hours and dangerous jobs; the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor (1886, Samuel Gompers) organized them; the Haymarket affair (1886), Homestead strike (1892) and Pullman strike (1894) turned violent and set back unions.
topics.trouble: Students think the government usually sided with strikers. In the major strikes of the era, courts issued injunctions and state or federal troops were sent, mostly against the strikers.

topics.title: New Immigrants and Growing Cities
topics.short: From the 1880s, most immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe, many through Ellis Island (opened 1892); cities filled with tenements, political machines such as Tammany Hall, and settlement houses such as Jane Addams's Hull House (1889); the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese laborers.
topics.trouble: Students think Ellis Island officials changed immigrants' names. Ships' lists were made at the port of departure; most name changes came later, made by the immigrants themselves.

topics.title: Gilded Age Politics and the Populists
topics.short: After President Garfield's assassination, the Pendleton Act (1883) began a merit-based civil service; the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) regulated railroads; struggling farmers formed the People's (Populist) Party (1892); in 1896 William McKinley (gold standard) defeated William Jennings Bryan (free silver).
topics.trouble: Students think the free-silver debate was about jewelry or coins only. It was about the money supply: farmers in debt wanted more money in circulation (and higher prices), while bankers and creditors favored the gold standard.

topics.title: Jim Crow and Plessy v. Ferguson
topics.short: Southern states passed segregation laws and kept Black citizens from voting with poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses; in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) the Supreme Court upheld "separate but equal" 7 to 1, over Justice John Marshall Harlan's dissent; Ida B. Wells campaigned against lynching.
topics.trouble: Students think separate facilities were in fact equal under Plessy. The facilities provided for Black citizens were almost always worse; the doctrine was overturned for public schools by Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

topics.title: Ideas of the Gilded Age
topics.short: People argued over the new wealth: Carnegie's "Gospel of Wealth" (the rich should give it away well), Social Darwinism (competition sorts the fit), the Social Gospel (faith calls for reform), and Booker T. Washington's and W. E. B. Du Bois's different strategies for Black advancement.
topics.trouble: Students think Washington and Du Bois agreed. Washington stressed vocational education and economic progress first; Du Bois demanded full civil and political rights and higher education now.

topics.title: Becoming a World Power
topics.short: American planters and businessmen in Hawaii helped overthrow Queen Liliuokalani (1893), and the U.S. annexed Hawaii in 1898; the Spanish-American War (1898) brought Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where a long war against Filipino independence fighters followed (1899 to 1902); Americans debated empire sharply.
topics.trouble: Students think the war with Spain was fought only in Cuba. It began over Cuba, but American forces also fought in the Philippines and took Puerto Rico and Guam.

topics.title: The Open Door, the Big Stick and the Canal
topics.short: The U.S. sought an Open Door for trade in China (1899); Theodore Roosevelt backed Panama's independence and built the Panama Canal (opened 1914) and added the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) to the Monroe Doctrine; Taft favored "dollar diplomacy."
topics.trouble: Students mix up the policies by president. Roosevelt: Big Stick and the Corollary; Taft: dollar diplomacy (investment); Wilson: "moral diplomacy," though he too sent troops to the Caribbean and Mexico.

topics.title: Muckrakers and Reformers
topics.short: Journalists called muckrakers exposed problems: Jacob Riis (city slums), Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil), Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (meatpacking, 1906); Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act in 1906.
topics.trouble: Students think Sinclair wrote The Jungle to expose food safety. He meant to show workers' lives; readers reacted most to the meat. ("I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach.")

topics.title: The Progressive Presidents
topics.short: Theodore Roosevelt broke up trusts and protected forests and parks; Taft continued antitrust suits; Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act (1913), the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act (1914).
topics.trouble: Students think Roosevelt opposed all big business. He distinguished "good" trusts from "bad" ones and preferred regulating most large companies to breaking them up.

topics.title: Progressive Amendments and Direct Democracy
topics.short: Four amendments came in seven years: the Sixteenth (income tax, 1913), Seventeenth (senators elected by voters, 1913), Eighteenth (Prohibition, 1919) and Nineteenth (women's suffrage, 1920); many states also adopted the initiative, referendum, recall and direct primary.
topics.trouble: Students think senators were always elected by voters. Until 1913 state legislatures chose them.

topics.title: Winning Women's Suffrage
topics.short: After decades of work by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony and others, Carrie Chapman Catt's NAWSA lobbied state by state while Alice Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House; the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in August 1920.
topics.trouble: Students think no woman voted anywhere before 1920. Wyoming let women vote from 1869 as a territory, and many Western states did before the amendment.

topics.title: The NAACP and the Great Migration
topics.short: The NAACP (1909) fought segregation in court and in public; from about 1910 to 1970 roughly six million Black Southerners moved to cities of the North and West for jobs and to escape Jim Crow.
topics.trouble: Students think the Great Migration happened all at once. It came in two big waves, around the World Wars, over six decades.

topics.title: The United States Enters the Great War
topics.short: The U.S. stayed neutral when war began in 1914; German submarine attacks (the Lusitania, 1915; unrestricted warfare, 1917) and the Zimmermann Telegram led Congress to declare war in April 1917.
topics.trouble: Students think the Lusitania sinking brought the U.S. into the war right away. It came two years before the U.S. entered; the renewed submarine campaign and the Zimmermann Telegram in 1917 were the immediate causes.

topics.title: The War at Home and the Peace
topics.short: The government drafted soldiers, ran wartime agencies and limited dissent (the Espionage Act, 1917; Schenck v. United States, 1919); the war ended with the armistice of November 11, 1918; Wilson's Fourteen Points and League of Nations failed to win the Senate's approval of the Treaty of Versailles.
topics.trouble: Students think the U.S. joined the League of Nations because Wilson proposed it. The Senate did not ratify the treaty, so the U.S. never joined.

topics.title: The Twenties
topics.short: Cars (the Model T), radio, movies and buying on credit created a mass consumer culture; jazz spread from New Orleans to Chicago and New York; the Harlem Renaissance (Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston) flourished.
topics.trouble: Students think everyone prospered in the 1920s. Farmers struggled all decade, and wealth grew most at the top.

topics.title: Conflicts of the Twenties
topics.short: The Red Scare (1919 to 1920), the Sacco and Vanzetti case, immigration quotas (1921, 1924), the Scopes trial (1925), a revived Ku Klux Klan and the struggle to enforce Prohibition showed a country divided over change.
topics.trouble: Students think Prohibition banned drinking alcohol. The Eighteenth Amendment banned making, selling and transporting it; it was repealed by the Twenty-first Amendment in 1933.

topics.title: The Crash of 1929
topics.short: Stocks crashed in October 1929 (Black Tuesday, October 29); historians and economists weigh several causes of the Depression that followed: speculation and buying on margin, bank failures, a shrinking money supply, overproduction, unequal income and high tariffs.
topics.trouble: Students think the Crash alone caused the Great Depression. Most economists see the Crash as one cause among several, and they debate how much weight to give each.

topics.title: Life in the Great Depression
topics.short: By 1933 about a quarter of workers were unemployed; thousands of banks failed; drought and dust storms drove families from the Plains (the Dust Bowl); Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation lent to banks and businesses, and the Bonus Army was driven from Washington (1932).
topics.trouble: Students think Hoover did nothing. He did more than earlier presidents in downturns (public works, the RFC) but opposed direct federal relief to individuals.

topics.title: The New Deal
topics.short: Franklin Roosevelt (from 1933) promised relief, recovery and reform: the CCC, the TVA, the WPA, deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933), the SEC (1934), Social Security and the Wagner Act (1935), and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938).
topics.trouble: Students mix up the three Rs. Relief helped people now (WPA jobs); recovery aimed to restart the economy; reform aimed to prevent another crash (FDIC, SEC).

topics.title: The New Deal and the Supreme Court
topics.short: The Court struck down parts of the New Deal (Schechter, 1935); Roosevelt's 1937 plan to add justices failed in Congress, but that year the Court began upholding economic regulation (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish; NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin).
topics.trouble: Students think the court-packing plan passed. Congress rejected it; the Court's rulings shifted anyway, and retirements soon let Roosevelt appoint new justices.

topics.title: Judging the New Deal
topics.short: Critics on the left (Huey Long, Father Coughlin) said the New Deal did too little; critics on the right (the American Liberty League) said it did too much; historians and economists still debate how much it helped recovery, while agreeing it changed the federal government's role for good.
topics.trouble: Students take one side's view as the agreed verdict. Present each view with its evidence: unemployment fell but stayed high until the war; programs such as Social Security and deposit insurance lasted.

topics.title: The Road to War
topics.short: Neutrality Acts (1935 to 1937) kept the U.S. out of foreign wars; after war began in Europe (1939), "cash and carry," Lend-Lease (1941) and the Atlantic Charter moved the country toward the Allies while isolationists argued against it.
topics.trouble: Students think the U.S. was at war from 1939. It sent aid but did not enter until December 1941, after Pearl Harbor.

topics.title: Pearl Harbor
topics.short: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii; Congress declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11.
topics.trouble: Students think the U.S. declared war on Germany first. The U.S. declared war on Japan; Germany declared war on the U.S. three days later.

topics.title: The Home Front
topics.short: Factories switched to war production; millions of women took industrial jobs; rationing, war bonds and scrap drives involved everyone; A. Philip Randolph's planned march won an order against discrimination in defense jobs (1941), and Black Americans pressed a "Double V" for victory abroad and at home.
topics.trouble: Students think women stayed in factory jobs after the war. Many were laid off or left as veterans returned, though women's paid work kept rising over the following decades.

topics.title: The Incarceration of Japanese Americans
topics.short: Executive Order 9066 (1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them U.S. citizens, to camps; the Supreme Court upheld the removal in Korematsu v. United States (1944); Congress apologized and paid redress in the Civil Liberties Act of 1988.
topics.trouble: Students think those incarcerated were mostly foreign nationals. About two-thirds were American citizens born in the United States.

topics.title: The War in Europe and the Holocaust
topics.short: The Allies fought in North Africa (1942), Sicily and Italy (1943), landed in Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944) and turned back Germany's last offensive at the Bulge; Germany surrendered on V-E Day (May 8, 1945); Allied soldiers liberated camps where Nazi Germany had murdered six million Jews and millions of others.
topics.trouble: Students think D-Day began the fighting in Europe. Americans had fought in North Africa and Italy since 1942 and 1943, and the Soviet Union had fought Germany in the East since 1941.

topics.title: The War in the Pacific
topics.short: After the turning point at Midway (June 1942), U.S. forces "island hopped" toward Japan (Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima, Okinawa); atomic bombs struck Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9); Japan announced surrender August 15 and signed it September 2.
topics.trouble: Students present the decision to use the bomb as settled one way or the other. Historians debate it: supporters stress the lives an invasion would have cost; critics point to Japan's weakening position and other options. Teach the evidence on each side.

topics.title: Planning the Peace
topics.short: At Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July 1945) the Allies planned postwar Europe; the United Nations was founded in 1945, with the U.S. as a permanent member of the Security Council.
topics.trouble: Students think the United Nations was the League of Nations renamed. The U.S. never joined the League; it helped found the UN and joined it in 1945.

topics.title: Containment
topics.short: The U.S. set out to contain Soviet communism: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe (1948), the Berlin Airlift (1948 to 1949) and the NATO alliance (1949).
topics.trouble: Students think the Cold War was a war of U.S. and Soviet armies fighting each other. The two never fought each other directly; they competed through alliances, aid, arms, space and wars fought by others or in other lands.

topics.title: The Second Red Scare
topics.short: Fear of Soviet spying (the Hiss and Rosenberg cases) led to loyalty programs, congressional hearings (HUAC) and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations (1950 to 1954) until the Senate censured him.
topics.trouble: Students think every accusation was false, or that there was no Soviet spying. Real Soviet espionage existed (as later records confirm), and many accusations against ordinary people were baseless.

topics.title: The Korean War
topics.short: North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950; UN forces led by the U.S. fought North Korean and later Chinese armies; an armistice in 1953 left Korea divided near the 38th parallel, with no peace treaty.
topics.trouble: Students think the Korean War ended with a peace treaty or a victory. It ended in an armistice, and Korea remains divided.

topics.title: The 1950s
topics.short: The GI Bill (1944), suburbs such as Levittown, the baby boom, television and the Interstate Highway Act (1956) reshaped life; the Soviet launch of Sputnik (1957) spurred new spending on science and education.
topics.trouble: Students think the 1950s were the same for every family. Suburbs often excluded Black families through restrictive covenants and lending practices, and poverty remained in cities and rural areas.

topics.title: Kennedy, Cuba and the Space Race
topics.short: The Bay of Pigs invasion failed (1961); the Berlin Wall went up (1961); in the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) the U.S. and the USSR came close to nuclear war before the Soviets removed their missiles; the space race led to Apollo 11's Moon landing (1969).
topics.trouble: Students think Kennedy saw the Moon landing. Kennedy set the goal in 1961 and was assassinated in 1963; the landing came in 1969, under Nixon.

topics.title: The Vietnam War
topics.short: After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964), U.S. troops in Vietnam grew to over 500,000; the Tet Offensive (1968) shook public support; protests spread at home (Kent State, 1970); the Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended U.S. combat, and Saigon fell in 1975; Congress passed the War Powers Resolution (1973).
topics.trouble: Students think Congress declared war on Vietnam. It never did; the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution authorized the President to use force, which is why the War Powers Resolution followed.

topics.title: The Great Society
topics.short: Lyndon Johnson's Great Society (1964 to 1966) included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid (1965), federal aid to schools and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended the national-origins quotas.
topics.trouble: Students mix up Medicare and Medicaid. Medicare covers people 65 and older; Medicaid covers people with low incomes.

topics.title: Nixon, Detente and Watergate
topics.short: Richard Nixon opened relations with China (1972), signed arms limits with the USSR (SALT I, 1972) and created the EPA (1970); the Watergate scandal and United States v. Nixon (1974) led to his resignation on August 9, 1974.
topics.trouble: Students think Nixon was impeached and removed. The House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment, but he resigned before the full House voted.

topics.title: The End of the Cold War
topics.short: Ronald Reagan built up defense and called on the Soviets to "tear down this wall" (1987); he and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty (1987); the Berlin Wall fell (November 9, 1989) and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
topics.trouble: Students credit a single person or cause. Historians weigh U.S. pressure, the Soviet economy's weakness, Gorbachev's reforms and the people of Eastern Europe; they debate the balance.

topics.title: Early Victories
topics.short: Jackie Robinson integrated major league baseball (1947); Truman ordered the armed forces desegregated (1948); Mendez v. Westminster (1947) ended the segregation of Mexican American children in California schools.
topics.trouble: Students think the movement began with Rosa Parks in 1955. Legal and political work went back decades, through the NAACP's lawsuits and wartime campaigns.

topics.title: Brown v. Board of Education
topics.short: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled 9 to 0 that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause, overturning Plessy for schools; resistance followed, and in 1957 Eisenhower sent troops to protect the Little Rock Nine.
topics.trouble: Students think schools desegregated right after Brown. The Court ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed" (1955), and many districts resisted for more than a decade.

topics.title: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
topics.short: After Rosa Parks's arrest in December 1955, Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, boycotted the buses for 381 days, led by Martin Luther King Jr.; in 1956 the courts ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.
topics.trouble: Students think the boycott was spontaneous. Local leaders and groups, including the Women's Political Council, had planned for such a protest and organized carpools to keep it going.

topics.title: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides and the March on Washington
topics.short: Students sat in at a Greensboro lunch counter (1960) and founded SNCC; Freedom Riders tested bus integration (1961); after the Birmingham campaign (1963) and King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," 250,000 people joined the March on Washington (August 28, 1963).
topics.trouble: Students think nonviolent protest meant passive protest. It was organized, trained and risky: protesters planned carefully and faced arrests and attacks.

topics.title: The Civil Rights Laws
topics.short: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in public places and jobs; the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; after the Selma marches, the Voting Rights Act (1965) ended literacy tests and brought federal oversight; the Fair Housing Act followed in 1968.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the 1964 and 1965 laws. The Civil Rights Act (1964) covered public places and jobs; the Voting Rights Act (1965) covered voting.

topics.title: Debates Within the Movement
topics.short: Leaders differed on methods and goals: King's nonviolent integration, Malcolm X's call for self-defense and Black pride, and the Black Power movement (from 1966); King was assassinated in April 1968.
topics.trouble: Students reduce the debate to "good" and "bad" leaders. Present each leader's argument in his own words and the circumstances behind it; Malcolm X's views also changed late in his life.

topics.title: Other Movements for Equal Rights
topics.short: Others drew on the movement: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta organized farmworkers (the UFW); the American Indian Movement (1968) pressed for treaty rights; the women's movement won Title IX (1972), though the Equal Rights Amendment was not ratified; the Americans with Disabilities Act passed in 1990.
topics.trouble: Students think the Equal Rights Amendment is part of the Constitution. Congress passed it in 1972, but it was not ratified by three-fourths of the states before its deadline, and its status remains disputed.

topics.title: The 1970s
topics.short: An oil embargo (1973) and "stagflation" (high inflation with high unemployment) strained the economy; Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon; Jimmy Carter brokered the Camp David Accords (1978) and faced the Iran hostage crisis (1979 to 1981).
topics.trouble: Students think inflation and unemployment always move in opposite directions. In the 1970s both were high at once, which puzzled policymakers.

topics.title: The Conservative Resurgence
topics.short: Ronald Reagan won in 1980 and 1984 on lower taxes, less regulation and a stronger defense; supporters credit his policies with the long expansion after 1982, while critics point to larger deficits and widening inequality.
topics.trouble: Students state one side's judgment as fact. Describe the policies and the record (tax cuts in 1981 and 1986, rising deficits, falling inflation), then each side's reading of them.

topics.title: A World After the Cold War
topics.short: The U.S. led a coalition in the Gulf War (1991), joined NAFTA (in force 1994), took part in NATO operations in Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999), and faced new questions about its role as the only superpower.
topics.trouble: Students think the end of the Cold War ended American military actions abroad. The 1990s saw several deployments under the UN and NATO.

topics.title: Computers, the Internet and a Global Economy
topics.short: Personal computers spread in the 1980s; the World Wide Web (1991) opened the internet to the public; trade and investment linked economies worldwide, and the country debated the gains and costs of globalization.
topics.trouble: Students think the internet and the Web are the same thing or both began in the 1990s. The internet grew from 1960s and 1970s research networks; the Web is a system for linked pages that runs on it, created in 1989 to 1991.

topics.title: Politics of the 1990s
topics.short: Bill Clinton (1993 to 2001) signed NAFTA and a 1996 welfare reform passed by a Republican Congress; the federal budget ran surpluses from 1998 to 2001; the House impeached Clinton in 1998 and the Senate acquitted him in 1999; the 2000 election was decided after Bush v. Gore.
topics.trouble: Students think impeachment means removal from office. The House impeaches (charges) and the Senate holds the trial; Clinton, like Andrew Johnson, was acquitted.

topics.title: The Nine Periods: Putting It Together
topics.short: Place events from 1491 to 2000 in their AP periods and in order, and explain a cause and an effect that link one period to the next.
topics.trouble: Students memorize events but cannot place them. Anchor each period with two or three dates (1607, 1754, 1800, 1848, 1877, 1898, 1945, 1980) and build out from them.
